name: Bianca Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift on the lines for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity company crew that builds and repairs power lines. My diploma taught me to read a network drawing, and years on site taught me to ask whose hand checked the isolation before anybody climbs. I like training a newer worker through a difficult fault, though I miss dinner with my partner and our two school-age children when a storm runs late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that routine AI might clean up a few depot forms. I use it now and then for a draft note, but the crew still checks a pole and signs the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher lineworker pay and more than six months of savings mean the mortgage is not at risk from a tidier form. I care more about a supervisor accepting a draft note without the crew’s signoff. A drafted AI note cannot sign for the line crew that checked the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the same repair shifts and compare any drafted note with the signed work sheet. During the first year I would have the apprentice read back the pole number before the report is filed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our living, with my usual eye on field safety. A mild change to forms barely reaches the work that earns my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes wrong if the apprentice skips the readback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two poles can share a street name, and the wrong number can send the next crew to the wrong fault. I would stop the report until the field sheet matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your household spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my partner and I can keep the mortgage and children’s costs as planned. We already have a strong cushion, and I do not expect this modest AI change to cut my shifts.

say: **Routine** AI may tidy depot notes while crews still sign and complete line repairs.
I would **keep** pole-number readbacks before filing a report.
think: Our **high** pay and strong savings keep a minor form change from threatening the mortgage.
An **unsigned** draft could mislead the next crew about the true fault.
do: **Keep** leading repair shifts and compare drafts with signed work sheets.
**Have** apprentice read back pole numbers before each report is filed.
feel: **Calm** about income, with steady attention to field safety.
S0.quote: A drafted AI note cannot sign for the line crew that checked the pole.
fieldNote: Her **occasional** AI use stays within paperwork and depends on signed physical records.
**Strong** savings and high pay support a calm household view in the mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and verify drafted notes against signed work sheets
Have apprentice read back pole numbers before filing reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that AI scheduling might shorten some waits, but crews need a way to challenge an impossible repair time. I would bring our union safety group into any trial before a new target becomes part of the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks in dispatch and buying change first, not the physical repair. My own hours look secure for now, but a faster plan can hide how long isolation and traffic control really take. A power line repair beside traffic starts before the first tool touches the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union safety group to collect a month of actual isolation and repair times, and I would help mark the hard cases. In the first year I would bring those figures to the company scheduling trial and keep the crew on its present site checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because targets can turn a good tool into a poor safety decision. I would welcome a trial if it treats field records as evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you mark as hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pole beside a busy road may need traffic control before the isolation check even starts. I would note that time separately from the actual repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask it to let a crew lead add a reason code when the schedule misses a hazard. Our union group could then compare those codes with the original estimates.

say: **AI** scheduling should allow crews to challenge impossible repair times.
I would **include** our union safety group in the trial.
think: **Dispatch** and buying change first while my lineworker hours appear secure.
A **tighter** plan may omit isolation and traffic control time.
do: **Collect** one month of isolation and repair times with the union group.
**Bring** marked hard cases to the company scheduling trial.
**Keep** present crew site checks while targets are tested.
feel: **Uneasy** about targets, though open to a trial grounded in field evidence.
S1.quote: A power line repair beside traffic starts before the first tool touches the pole.
fieldNote: She **uses** collective timing evidence to protect field judgment without claiming her own job is disappearing.
The **trial** has a defined record and correction route, not a blanket rejection of software.

steps.text: Collect one month of isolation and repair times with union safety group
Keep crew site checks while scheduling targets are trialled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could take dispatch decisions quickly, with capable line robots around 2031. The union should require paid field trials and clear responsibility for mistakes before any machine gets a live job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot could eventually reduce our callout hours, though I cannot say my lead post would go. We have over six months saved and plenty of nearby lineworker work, but losing high pay would still change the mortgage and children’s plans. A line robot needs a fault report with the weather in it, not only a clean demonstration film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would bring a paid trial and stop-work proposal to our union committee. In the first year after 2028 I would request a paid place on the company field test crew if the trial includes real fault reports, and compare our monthly callout earnings before changing the family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the speed, but not without choices. I want the workers doing the repairs to set the conditions for robot work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the fault report record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The report needs the pole, weather, attempted repair, crew intervention and who authorised a restart. A tidy demonstration clip tells us too little about a live street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What family plan might change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If callout pay actually drops for several months, my partner and I would postpone a planned school holiday. I would not cut it now on the strength of a scenario alone.

say: I would **seek** paid field trials and clear fault responsibility before robots work live lines.
**Thinking** AI may change dispatch by 2028, with capable line robots around 2031.
think: **Callout** hours might shrink, but strong savings and nearby employers leave room to respond.
**Losing** higher pay would affect mortgage and children’s plans if the decline lasts.
do: **Bring** paid trial and stop-work proposal to the union committee this year.
**Request** a paid company field test place after 2028 if real faults are recorded.
**Postpone** school holiday only if callout pay falls for several months.
feel: **Anxious** about speed, while aware of savings and local job options.
S2.quote: A line robot needs a fault report with the weather in it, not only a clean demonstration film.
fieldNote: She **distinguishes** a possible reduction in high callout pay from a certain job loss.
The **holiday** change depends on actual sustained earnings decline, not merely the card.

steps.text: Bring paid field trial and stop-work proposal to union committee
Postpone school holiday if callout pay falls for several months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us time to write proper trial standards. I would ask the union and company to publish failed line tests alongside successful ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into a paid field safety assessor post if the work still puts me at the pole. My diploma and crew lead record help, but I would want a real vacancy and a salary that covers our mortgage before leaving higher paid line work. A failed line robot test should be filed where the next crew can read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union training committee this year for the company’s assessor course terms and posted pay scale. If the course is funded on paid time and a local field assessor opening matches my current pay, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the post is open; otherwise I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end point, but the extra years make the terms testable. I will learn a new job when it is a paid field job, not a title on a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failed test would you want published?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want any test where a robot misses a damaged crossarm or moves before isolation is confirmed. The next crew deserves the failure record, not only the sales result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the assessor role is unpaid at first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain on the line and ask the union to bargain for paid training. Our savings are strong, but a temporary unpaid promise is not how I would protect the family mortgage.

say: The **longer** lead allows open records of failed line robot tests before 2034.
I would **seek** jointly agreed field standards with the union and company.
think: A **paid** field assessor role might fit my diploma if a real local vacancy exists.
**Higher** line pay and the mortgage make salary matching a firm condition.
do: **Ask** union training committee for funded course and assessor salary terms.
**Enroll** before 2031 if course is paid and local assessor post matches pay.
**Apply** when a suitable field assessor vacancy is actually posted.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual robots, but able to test job terms in advance.
S3.quote: A failed line robot test should be filed where the next crew can read it.
fieldNote: She would **consider** a career shift after paid training and an actual comparable offer.
The **union** role is to secure records and terms; her own savings do not replace wages.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded course and local matching-pay vacancy exist
Apply for posted field assessor role if salary matches current pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before full thinking AI and three more years before capable robots lets apprentices learn both physical repairs and machine limits. I would keep experienced crews involved in teaching at real sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I might prefer fewer night callouts, but I cannot promise the mortgage will be gone. A paid apprenticeship supervisor role could fit if its hours and pay are real; I am not planning to leave work altogether. A line apprentice needs to find the damaged hardware before reading a robot’s plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company and union training group about paid apprentice supervisor posts and their hours. If an actual opening later offers pay that meets our household needs, I would apply in the first year after 2036 while keeping my line shifts until an offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about having time to choose. I can stay with the crew, teach more, or consider a posted role once the family budget is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have an apprentice do before seeing the robot plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have them identify the isolation points and damaged hardware at the pole. Then they could compare the machine’s plan with what their own eyes found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of a pay cut could the household take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot give a number ten years ahead. My partner and I would look at the remaining mortgage and the actual supervisor offer before agreeing to fewer callouts.

say: A **decade** lets apprentices learn physical repair and machine limits before robots arrive around 2039.
**Experienced** lineworkers should teach on real sites.
think: A **paid** apprenticeship supervisor role may suit later life if hours and salary work.
The **future** mortgage balance is unknown, and I do not plan to stop working.
do: **Ask** company and union training group about real supervisor posts this year.
**Apply** after 2036 if a posted paid supervisor role covers household costs.
**Keep** line shifts until an actual suitable offer arrives.
feel: **Calm** with time to choose field work or paid teaching.
S4.quote: A line apprentice needs to find the damaged hardware before reading a robot’s plan.
fieldNote: She **ends** with conditional paid teaching rather than automatic retirement or speculative retraining.
Her **strong** cushion and local options support calm when the timeline extends a decade.

steps.text: Apply after 2036 if posted supervisor role covers household costs
Keep line shifts until suitable supervisor offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach live repairs around 2031 before crews have agreed on safety records and responsibility. Paid trials with published failures, crew stop-work authority and notice of callout changes would help. My savings can cover a gap; they cannot tell a line robot when a wet pole is unsafe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the failure report after a trial. The next crew should see it, and the apprentices should learn what went wrong on a real job. An employer can buy a machine, but it still owes workers an honest record.

headlineQuote: My savings can cover a gap; they cannot tell a line robot when a wet pole is unsafe.
portrait: **Bianca** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and strong habits around signed isolation and field records.
**Higher** pay, over six months of savings and many nearby lineworker posts support her partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
She **uses** AI occasionally, accepts tested tools and presses her union to keep field evidence and worker authority in decisions.
She **considers** paid assessor or apprentice supervisor roles only when actual local offers and household pay conditions make them viable.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots around 2031 before crews agree on trial records and safe responsibility.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** trials with published failures, crew stop-work authority and early notice of callout changes would help her plan.
